title: Elul: letters of apology
hookLine: many write or call to apologize before the High Holy Days
tomorrow: a fish head on a holiday table? there's a wish inside it.

cards: Some messages sit in versions for weeks, the ones that start, hey, about what I said. In Elul, people finally send them: letters, calls, a knock on a door. Here's why the timing matters.
The Mishnah says Yom Kippur atones for a great deal, but there's one kind of wrong it can't fix on its own. Not by fasting, not by praying all day. Which one?

teach.h: THE DAY ATONES BETWEEN YOU AND GOD.
teach.b: Here's the Mishnah's answer. For wrongs between a person and God, Yom Kippur atones.

For wrongs between a person and another person, Yom Kippur does not atone until they make peace with the one they hurt. The day can't do your apologizing for you. That's why Elul fills with letters and calls.
And the Talmud adds a story about the other side.

teach.h: RABBI ZEIRA WALKS BY ON PURPOSE.
teach.b: When someone had wronged Rabbi Zeira, he would walk back and forth in front of that person, on purpose, so they'd have an easy chance to come and make it right. The hurt one makes the door easy to open.
Now a neighbor who says it too.

Owen's tradition keeps a saying of Jesus in Matthew: "first be reconciled to thy brother, and then come and offer thy gift." If you remember at the altar that someone has something against you, leave the gift and go.
Shared ground: make peace with the person before you come before God. And one honest difference. Matthew's saying names no season; it happens whenever the gift is brought.
The Jewish calendar also gives it a season and a date: a month to prepare, and a day it has to be done before. Something to tell a friend tonight: Rabbi Zeira made himself easy to apologize to.

how: In the weeks before Yom Kippur, Jews traditionally ask forgiveness of family, friends and coworkers, in person, by letter or by phone; some say a general request for forgiveness on the eve of Yom Kippur as well.

o: the day of fasting when all wrongs are forgiven
the month when people apologize before Yom Kippur
a prayer asking God to forgive the whole community

games.q: before the day — tap the pairs.
p: walked by so they could apologize
first be reconciled to thy brother

s: Yom Kippur atones for wrongs against other people automatically
the Mishnah says not until you make peace with the one you hurt.
both the Mishnah and a saying of Jesus put making peace with people first
Judaism and Christianity say exactly the same thing about apology
both put the person first; the Jewish calendar also gives it a season and a day.

games.q: your brother says he'll fast hard on Yom Kippur, and that will cover what he said to your dad. what does the Mishnah say?
o: the day covers wrongs against God; with Dad, he has to make peace first.
a sincere enough fast covers wrongs against people too.
he should wait for Dad to bring it up, then apologize.
games.why: Mishnah Yoma 8:9: for wrongs between people, Yom Kippur does not atone until they make peace. and Rabbi Zeira shows the other side: make it easy for them to come.

practice: Choose one person you owe an apology. Write the first two lines by hand: name what you did, plainly, without an if or a but. You don't have to send it today; Elul gives you time to get it right.

wordCard.voice: Elul: the month for apologies, because Yom Kippur covers wrongs against God, and waits on wrongs against people.

orig.note: Hebrew: until he makes peace with his fellow, from Mishnah Yoma 8:9.

carryVoice: Your line: apologize before the day. The day can't do it for you. Until tomorrow.

sources.ref: Mishnah Yoma 8:9 (Yom Kippur atones between a person and God; between people, not until one appeases the other)
Babylonian Talmud, Yoma 87a (Rabbi Zeira passes back and forth before one who wronged him)

sources.q: first be reconciled to thy brother, and then come and offer thy gift.
